query: Casting is the predominant fabrication method for high-entropy alloys, but solidification-related porosity and microstructural nonuniformity can cause heterogeneous properties. Studies of other high-entropy-alloy compositions have reported high hardness and notable compressive performance, yet these findings do not establish how to improve CoCrFeNiTi; moreover, some investigated alloys were brittle at 25 °C and displayed only limited plastic deformation at 600 °C. For equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi with a simple crystal structure, favorable plasticity and machinability, but low hardness and load-bearing capability, what single intervention could improve hardness and mechanical performance while preserving those favorable characteristics and clarifying the relationship between microstructure and deformation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, a quantitative prediction relative to the unmodified alloy, the processing and testing boundaries within which it should apply, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled microstructural and mechanical experiment with explicit falsification criteria.

generation.hypothesis: The introduction of a controlled amount of carbon (C) as an alloying element into equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloy through powder metallurgy will improve its hardness and mechanical performance while preserving favorable plasticity and machinability.
generation.material_initial_state: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloy with a simple crystal structure
generation.intervention: Addition of a controlled amount of carbon (C) as an alloying element
generation.conditions: Powder metallurgy processing, subsequent heat treatment to ensure homogenization and precipitation hardening, with processing temperatures between 1000°C to 1200°C
generation.mechanism: Precipitation hardening due to the formation of carbide precipitates, which will act as obstacles to dislocation movement, thereby enhancing the alloy's hardness and mechanical performance
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in hardness by at least 15% and an improvement in yield strength by at least 10% compared to the unmodified alloy, while maintaining a ductility of at least 5% elongation at break
generation.baseline: Unmodified equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloy
generation.uncertainty: The optimal amount of carbon addition and the precise heat treatment conditions required to achieve the desired microstructure and properties are uncertain and may require further experimentation to determine

falsification_experiment.design: Controlled experiment comparing the microstructure and mechanical properties of unmodified CoCrFeNiTi with the carbon-modified alloy, using techniques such as scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), hardness testing, and tensile testing
measurements: Hardness (HV), yield strength (YS), ultimate tensile strength (UTS), elongation at break (EB)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the carbon-modified alloy does not exhibit at least a 10% increase in hardness and a 5% increase in yield strength compared to the unmodified alloy, or if the ductility (elongation at break) is reduced below 5%, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure [1] – [3] . These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C [4] , [5] . Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm 3 ) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added [6] – [13] . This paper reports the microstructural evolution and mechanical properties of a low-density Al 0.3 NbTa 0.8 Ti 1.5 V 0.2 Zr refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) prepared by means of a combination of mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering (SPS). Prior to sintering, the morphology, chemical homogeneity and crystal structures of the powders were thoroughly investigated by varying the milling times to find optimal conditions for densification. The sintered bulk RHEAs were produced with diverse feedstock powder conditions. The microstructural development of the materials was analyzed in terms of phase composition and constitution, chemical homogeneity, and crystallographic properties. Hardness and elastic constants also were measured. The calculation of phase diagrams (CALPHAD) was performed to predict the phase changes in the alloy, and the results were compared with the experiments. Milling time seems to play a significant role in the contamination level of the sintered materials. Even though a protective atmosphere was used in the entire manufacturing process, carbide formation was detected in the sintered bulks as early as after 3 h of powder milling.
